extracted.intended_audience: students writing a Third Year Project, Honours thesis, or Postgraduate Coursework project in the School of Mathematics & Statistics (UNSW)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing third-year project reports, honours theses, or postgraduate coursework project theses in mathematics and statistics: topic selection, supervision, writing style, structure, referencing, and academic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early topic and supervisor selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you start your Honours or Project year, speak to staff about possible thesis topics and try to settle on a topic and supervisor before the start of the first semester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find staff who work in areas you are interested in and who you find easy to talk mathematics with. Early agreement on topic/supervisor helps planning and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisor engagement and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Supervisors are expected to help select and modify the topic, direct you to useful references, explain difficult points, provide feedback on research direction, read and comment on drafts, help prepare for talks, and give general course advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most students see their supervisor about once a week (negotiable). Even if you haven't done much between visits, regular meetings let the supervisor keep track of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis purpose and target audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the thesis as an overview of what you have been studying and explain the area to a fellow student; your broad audience will be fellow Masters and Honours students who may not be experts in your topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an introduction explaining the project and its contents; a conclusion or summary is often appropriate. As Halmos advises, write for someone and anticipate/avoid the reader's difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and self-containment
rubrics_metrics.description: The thesis should be a coherent, self-contained piece of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the document stands alone: definitions, notation, main results and proofs should be presented so a competent reader can follow without external material not referenced where used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear introduction and appropriate conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an introduction that explains what the project is about and what its contents are; include a conclusion or summary where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be better to write the introduction towards the end of drafting. The introduction should orient the reader to goals, context, and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: High standards of English and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing should conform to the highest standards of English: clarity, precision and correct grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start sentences with capital letters and end them with full-stops. Don't start sentences with a symbol. Pay attention to diction, notation and punctuation. 'Good English style implies correct grammar, correct choice of words, correct punctuation, and, perhaps above all, common sense.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful bibliographic referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever material has an external source, this should be clear; give references for material wherever it is used and don't pad the reference list with uncited works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check current journals for acceptable referencing styles. Avoid statements like 'This report contains material from [1],[2] and [3]' without in-text linkage. Provide precise citations at points where external facts/ideas are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding plagiarism and academic honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports must be written in your own words; if you include a fact or idea that is not your own, the reader should be able to tell where you got it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that in mathematics there is a limit to how different a proof's basic structure can be, but you must still indicate sources. Familiarise yourself with the University's policies on academic honesty and plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of LaTeX for mathematical typesetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics reports and theses are almost always typed in LaTeX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow time to become familiar with LaTeX before writing; learning it well ahead of time is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time management and multiple drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not underestimate the time needed to produce a polished document; expect to produce several drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's difficult to fix mathematics, spelling, grammar and layout all at once. Get another student to proofread for fresh perspective and to catch issues you overlook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have something to say (substance over form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important ingredient of good exposition is to have something to say — an important idea or result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if exposition is imperfect, an important idea can carry the work; however, relying solely on this is rarely possible and not desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organise material to aid the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Organise and arrange material so as to minimize the reader's resistance and maximize their insight; keep the reader on track without unintended distractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good organization is the main contribution of an expository writer. Provide an outline and order material logically to build understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and consistency of notation ('think about the alphabet')
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest time in choosing the letters and notation you will use; a good, consistent notation can greatly aid understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan notation early; consistent notation prevents confusion and saves headaches later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative writing process ('write in spirals')
rubrics_metrics.description: Write chapters in an iterative order (1,2,1,2,3,1,2,3,4, ...), revising earlier chapters as later ones expose weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to revisit and rewrite earlier sections multiple times as the thesis develops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to mechanical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Be willing to work hard on mechanical details such as diction, notation, and punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical accuracy supports clarity; pay careful attention to grammar, punctuation and consistent notation throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek and use additional writing resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult recommended guides on writing mathematics for further practical advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists resources such as P. R. Halmos (How to write mathematics), Lee (A guide to writing mathematics; Some notes on writing mathematics), Jackson (Some notes on writing in mathematics), and Reiter (Writing a research paper in mathematics). Use these for deeper guidance on exposition and structure.
